text.en: Tamanna has two chocolates of different sizes. She says one-third of one chocolate is bigger than one-half of the other. Can that be true? It can, and we will see why.

A fraction names equal parts of a whole. If a whole is cut into 3 equal parts, each part is one-third.
When we compare two fractions of two different wholes, the two wholes must be the same size. One-third of a big chocolate can be bigger than one-half of a very small one.
Look at a grid. Shade one-third of grid A in red, one-half of grid B in blue and one-fourth of grid C in yellow. The size of a part depends on the whole.
The top number of a fraction, the numerator, tells how many parts we take. The bottom number tells into how many equal parts the whole is divided.
Parts must be equal. If the pieces are unequal then each piece is not called one-half or one-third.
The book also shows fractions greater than one. 5 pieces of a paratha cut into halves is 5 halves, which is 2 whole parathas and half more.
On a number line, the space between 0 and 1 holds the fractions smaller than one, and the fractions greater than one are placed to the right of 1.
From the book's opening: Tamanna has two chocolates of different sizes and says one-third of one is bigger than one-half of the other. To compare two fractions of two wholes, the wholes they come from must be the same.
Playing with a grid: shade 1/8 of Grid A in red, 1/6 of Grid B in blue and 1/12 of Grid C in yellow, and see if you can spot 1/3 in any of the grids.
With a fraction kit, a whole can be made using two different fraction pieces. One piece of 1/2 and two pieces of 1/4 make a whole, which shows that 1/2 = 2/4. When a 1/2 piece is broken into 2 equal parts, each part is a 1/4 piece.
Fraction kit tasks: make a whole using only 1/6 and 1/12 pieces, or 1/12, 1/4 and 1/2 pieces, or any five pieces of the same size, or any seven pieces of the same size.

problem.en: Raman's father cuts parathas into halves. Maa ate 5 pieces. How many parathas did she eat?

text.en: One piece is one-half of a paratha.
5 pieces make 5 halves, 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2.
Two pieces make one whole, so 5 halves is 2 and a half parathas.

why.en: Group pairs of halves into wholes.

prompt.en: Can one-third of a chocolate be bigger than half of another chocolate?

requiredIdeas.en: Yes, if the wholes are different sizes
Fractions of different wholes cannot be compared directly

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the bigger denominator always means a bigger piece

points.en: A fraction names equal parts of a whole.
Compare fractions only when the wholes are the same.
Fractions can be greater than one, like 5 halves.
